questions.prompt: Why is reading a[i] from an array O(1)?

options.text: The element's address is computed as base + i·w, independent of i and n
The array keeps a hash table mapping indices to values
The array scans from the front but stops early

questions.explanation: Contiguous storage means element i lives at a directly computable address, so access is constant-time arithmetic — no scanning or hashing.

questions.prompt: Appending to a dynamic array is O(1) amortized. What makes the amortized bound hold?

options.text: Capacity grows by a constant factor, so total resize work over n appends is O(n)
Each append grows the array by exactly one slot
The array is stored as a linked list

questions.explanation: Geometric growth makes resizes exponentially rare; the copies form a geometric series bounded by O(n), so the average per append is O(1).

questions.prompt: Which operations on a Python list of length n are O(n)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Front insert and front pop shift every following element (O(n)); membership scans the list (O(n)). Index assignment a[i] = x is O(1).

questions.prompt: Averaging the cost of an occasional O(n) resize over many cheap appends is called ______ analysis. (one word)
questions.explanation: Amortized analysis gives a worst-case average cost per operation across a sequence — here O(1) per append despite individual O(n) resizes.

questions.prompt: Order the steps a dynamic array takes when you append to a full array.

items.text: Allocate a new, larger backing block
Copy the existing elements into the new block
Store the new element in the next slot

questions.explanation: On a full array you must allocate a bigger block and copy across before there is room to store the new element and bump the size.

questions.prompt: Match each list operation with its time complexity.
questions.explanation: Indexing is constant, append is amortized constant, front insert is linear, and a slice copies the selected elements.
